## Traversal — running time {.smaller .smallcode}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
$T(n)$: running time of a traversal on a tree with $n$ nodes.

$T(0) = 1$

$T(n) = T(n_L) + T(n_R) + 1,\; n > 0.$

**Thm:** $T(n) = 2n + 1,\; n \ge 0.$
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```cpp
template<class T>
void tree<T>::preOrder(Node * croot) {
    if (croot != nullptr) {
        cout << croot->data;
        preOrder(croot->left);
        preOrder(croot->right);
    }
}
```

::::

::: notes
$n_L$ and $n_R$ are the sizes of the left and right subtrees, so
$n_L + n_R = n - 1$. Note $T(0) = 1$: calling on an empty tree still costs
one check.

**Proof**, by strong induction on $n$.

**Base case**, $n = 0$: $T(0) = 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1$. ✓

**IH:** $T(j) = 2j + 1$ for all $j < n$.

**Step**, $n > 0$: both subtrees are smaller than $n$, so

$$T(n) = (2n_L + 1) + (2n_R + 1) + 1 = 2(n_L + n_R + 1) + 1 = 2n + 1.$$

Where does the "$+1$" come from? The $n + 1$ calls on empty subtrees — the
null pointers from Monday's theorem. $n$ real calls plus $n + 1$ empty ones
is $2n + 1$. Any traversal is $\Theta(n)$.
:::

```cpp
template<class T>
void tree<T>::levelOrder(Node * croot) {










}
```
:::
::::

::: notes
Level order: `+ - * / d e b c`. Top to bottom, left to right — so it can't
follow the recursion. It needs a **queue**.

1. Make a queue; enqueue the root (if it isn't null).
2. While the queue isn't empty:
   a) dequeue a node, `t`;
   b) visit `t`, then
      i. enqueue `t->left` if it isn't null;
      ii. enqueue `t->right` if it isn't null.

```
Queue<Node *> q;
if (croot != nullptr) q.push(croot);
while (!q.isEmpty()) {
    Node * t = q.pop();
    cout << t->data;
    if (t->left  != nullptr) q.push(t->left);
    if (t->right != nullptr) q.push(t->right);
}
```

**This is PA2.** `components()` and `computeDistances()` are this loop, with
"neighbours on the map" in place of "children". Enqueue something only the
first time you see it — a map, unlike a tree, can lead you back to a node.
:::

1. We've studied 4 but…

\

2. Running time

::: notes
1. **…really two kinds.** Pre-, in- and postorder all go *deep* first: they
   ride the call stack (a stack!). Level order goes *wide* first: it rides a
   queue. Depth-first vs breadth-first — the same split we'll meet again on
   graphs.
2. All four visit each node once: $\Theta(n)$.
:::

## ADT Dictionary {.smaller .smallcode}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Suppose we have the following data…

| locker # | Name |
|---|---|
| 103 | Jay Hathaway |
| 92 | Linda Stencel |
| 330 | Bonnie Cook |
| 46 | Rick Brown |
| 124 | Kim Petersen |
| … | … |

…and we want to be able to retrieve a name, given a locker number.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
More examples of key/value pairs:

- CWL → Advising record
- Course number → Schedule info
- Color → PNG
- Vertex → Set of incident edges
- Flight number → Arrival information
- URL → html page

\

A dictionary is a structure supporting:

```cpp
void insert(kType & k, dType & d)
void remove(kType & k)
dType find(kType & k)
```
:::
::::

::: notes
Keys are unique; each one maps to its data. Every example on the right is a
real system's core: a CWL lookup, a flight board, the web itself.
:::

## ADT Dictionary: implementation options… {.smaller}

| | insert | find | (find +) remove |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **linked list** | $\Theta(1)$ | $\Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n) + \Theta(1)$ |
| **unsorted array** | $\Theta(1)$ | $\Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n) + \Theta(1)$ |
| **sorted array** | $\Theta(\log n) + \Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(\log n)$ | $\Theta(\log n) + \Theta(n)$ |
| **Binary Tree?** | | | |

::: notes
Linked list and unsorted array: insert anywhere, but find has to look at
everything. Sorted array: binary search finds in $\log n$, but inserting and
removing shift everything over. Nothing is fast at all three.

The last row is the question for next time: can a tree get $\log n$ for all
three? (Sometimes. That "sometimes" is the next two weeks.)
:::
